utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84bis-PT, the Prosecutor versus Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Can we have appearances for the day, please, starting with the the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honour. Paul Rogers appearing for the Prosecution, together with Aditya Menon and Ms. Elena Martin, and our Case Manager today, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence, starting with Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Ben Emmerson appearing for Ramush Haradinaj, together with Mr. Rod Dixon, assisted by Ms. Annie O'Reilly and Mr. Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Gregor Guy-Smith, Colleen Rohan, Chad Mair, and Gantian Zyberi on behalf of Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Paul Troop appearing for Mr. Brahimaj, assisted by Ms. Sophie Rigney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. This is the first time we are meeting in the new year and I know it's very deep into the year, but let me take this opportunity just to welcome you back and wish you a happy new year. This is a very small courtroom for this kind of people. Is everybody comfortable, particularly on that side? You are okay. Thank you so much. Well, now, pursuant to Rule 65 bis A of the rule, the purpose of a Status Conference is to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for trial and review the status of this case and to allow the accused to raise issues, including issues related to his mental and physical condition. This is the third Status Conference in this case. Now, the last Status Conference was held on the 26th of October, 2010, and this Status Conference is being held now because Rule 65 bis A requires that a Status Conference should be held within 120 days of the last Status Conference. It is, however, important to raise the implications of the Trial Chamber's decision on application on behalf of Ramush Haradinaj for certification pursuant to Rule 73 B. Until the Appeals Chamber decides on appeal on the Haradinaj Defence, there will be uncertainty about the scope of the indictment and about which witnesses the trial Chamber should here. This plainly limits the effective planning that can be made for the trial in the interim. In addition to that, the Balaj Defence also filed a motion for certification to appeal the Trial Chamber's decision on clarification of indictment. These two appeals overlap and they deal with issues which really are putting brakes on what can be done pending the appeal. I don't know whether the parties have any comments to make on this issue. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's obviously correct to say that pending the outcome of the Haradinaj appeal in particular, there are unanswered questions as to the scope of the retrial. But it's also right to say, if I can put this matter, so to speak, on the opposite pole or in the opposite side of the scale, that this was a trial which was expected to begin on or around the 24th of January, that Mr. Haradinaj is in pre-trial custody, and that he remains in custody despite originally a decision of the Trial Chamber to admit him to provisional release. On the clear understanding that the trial would proceed swiftly. It was then and remains now his imperative that this trial should begin as early as possible, but of course, subject to the competing imperative that it should be confined within the proper scope of the retrial that the Appeals Chamber has ordered. And I put those two competing considerations before the Trial Chamber because whilst it's right to say that certain important questions about the the scope of the trial and the nature of the evidence to be called remain yet to be determined, it does not, in our submission, follow that the continued preparation for trial, both of the parties and with the assistance of the Trial Chamber, should stop. Because if that happens at this stage, there will inevitably be a delay until the Appeals Chamber judgement is handed down, and once handed down if it is only then that the the parties are enabled to proceed with their preparation for trial, then there will inevitably be yet further delay whilst the steps that are necessary to be completed take place, and in particular I have in mind the disclosure to the Defence of the axiom at the centre of the Prosecution's case on the retrial which requires investigation. That involves lifting of redactions on the forenamed witnesses in the first of two outstanding motions and the background disclosure material in respect of Witness 81, that is the second motion. There is no reason in principle while the Trial Chamber cannot now rule upon those motions. If the Trial Chamber were to do so and to grant them, the time that is being occupied by the Appeals Chamber, can at the same time be occupied by the parties in being ready for trial, in order to secure the objective that once the Appeals Chamber judgement is handed down, we are ready to go. That is to say, all parties are ready to go. And in our submission, that is something which serves the proper administration of justice in part because further continued delay whilst the accused are in custody is unjust. And so whilst it's right to say that if one proceeds on the strictest order of business, one would wish the outcome of the appeals judgement to be known before one ruled or invited the Trial Chamber to rule, on the substance of all outstanding motions, there is in principle no reason why the Trial Chamber cannot make those rulings now, and if the Trial Chamber does not make those rulings now, the consequence is going to be at least a months and probably two months additional delay all of which is capable of being avoided given that the accused are in custody. And that is not with respect an irrelevant consideration. The Trial Chamber has taken the view that given the delay that had already taken place an order for provisional release was the right result. The Appeals Chamber has overturned that decision, but it cannot be the case that either the Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber, certainly not the Defence, and one would hope not the Prosecution, are indifferent to the interrelationship between avoidable delay and continued pre-trial detention. This is pre-trial detention with respect to the man who was on provisional release all the way through the original trial and was then acquitted. Is the delay avoidable? Answer, we respectfully submit plainly it is. It's avoidable by the Trial Chamber ruling on the two outstanding motions. And in our submission that is the right course now to pursue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Guy-Smith, anything you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I think you meant Mr. Rogers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon wasn't invited to have another go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we recognise of course there is a balancing exercise to be undertaken and Your Honour and Your Honours colleagues have before you all the applications and the arguments in relation to them, and Your Honours, of course, will recognise that there is a balance to be struck. The Prosecution is certainly not indifferent to accused persons sitting in custody awaiting their trial. However, my learned friends have made an application that one of the central tenets to which is that the case should be restricted. They also make an application for disclosure relating to a witness they say should not be admitted. And so far as he is concerned, Your Honours have before you information which indicates that there may be risks to that individual, risks to others. That is part of the balancing exercise that Your Honours have to undertake in determining whether a delayed disclosure application should be granted in relation to that individual. Of course, if the Appeals Chamber were to rule that that evidence should not be admitted, there is a risk that that individual could be exposed to unnecessary risk to himself, likewise to the others. It's part of the balance which Your Honours have to take into account, and the issues relating to that have been set out and no doubt the Court will determine what the right course of action is. But certainly we are not indifferent, and I would hope it wasn't being suggested that we were. I don't think Mr. Emmerson was suggesting we are indifferent. In relation to other disclosure matters, I have last evening sent out to my learned friends a response to their various other requests, it's an additional response to one I'd already provided. There are some outstanding disclosure matters that we can attend to. We are certainly mindful of that and are progressing it to the best of our ability given the outstanding motions that exist. So the Prosecution is very mindful of its obligations. We've litigated where we disagree. We responded, I hope my learned friends would agree, swiftly to the various requests and some delays but not excessive, and we are progressing into litigation where disagreements arise. So I think the the parties are doing the best they can to progress issues, but we respectfully agree with Your Honour that at this stage of affairs at the moment with outstanding appeals does somewhat put the Trial Chamber in some strait jacket to some extent on how it further progresses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, with respect, can't be simultaneously conducting a balance, as Mr. Rogers says it is, and yet be in a strait jacket. The right analogy is a balance, and the only factor that Mr. Rogers puts in the balance against proceeding to rule on these motions now is the suggestion that were the Appeals Chamber to determine that Witness 81 - and let us focus on him for a moment - should not be called at the retrial, the Trial Chamber would have made an order for disclosure in relation to a witness who was not then to be called. What's wrong with that? Well, says Mr. Rogers, that might expose the witness to risks which are risks that should properly be taken if he is going to be called but need not be taken if he is not going to be called. So that, if I may put it this way, significantly reduced consideration is the only matter Mr. Rogers is in a position to put into the balance on that side of the scale. To which the answer is a very simply one, this is a request for disclosure only to the Defence. That will be subject to a range of restrictions, culled from the restrictions that were imposed by the previous Trial Chamber at the suggestion of the Defence on the disclosure of information in respect of protected witnesses at the original trial. There is not now nor could there be the slightest suggestion that those acting for Mr. Haradinaj or Mr. Haradinaj himself or any one on his behalf or in respect of either of the other accused, any individual, is shown to have interfered with witnesses. Each and every one of the provisional release decisions successively throughout the original trial and thereafter has emphasised, certainly in respect of Mr. Haradinaj, that there is no suggestion of improper conduct by the Defence or the accused or those acting on his instructions or behalf in respect of witness interference. That being the case, there is in reality nothing to put into the scales on the side of delay and every imperative to enable the trial to be ready once the Appeal Chamber gives clear directions as to its scope. And let us be under no misunderstanding, the Defence intends to investigate Witness 81 properly and with appropriate safeguards but to investigate. The Defence carried out such an investigation in respect of Witness 80, and the material that it revealed, which will in due course potentially be adduced during the trial will, we submit, demonstrate to the Trial Chamber the witness is manifestly unreliable and a similar investigation is inevitable in respect of Witness 81. It will happen. And that being the case, in our submission, to put matters back so that we now wait another five or six weeks for the appeal judgement, then the Trial Chamber lifts the redactions, and then we have a month or two months of further investigation, places the start of this trial a good six months later than it was envisaged. Six months during which Mr. Haradinaj remains in custody despite having been provisionally released throughout the proceedings to date and acquitted of all counts by the original Trial Chamber. That, with respect, would be an unjust result and one which is eminently avoidable with effective trial management to secure the proper interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: My learned friend indicates.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please use the long microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I have the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The longer microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Oh, forgive me. Okay. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Interpreter, is that better? Or whoever intervened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, it is better, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'll try to move to the long microphone. Your Honours, my learned friend refers to one balancing exercise and one factor which I put into the balance, as he put it. Your Honours, of course the other one, which I didn't mention, is that my learned friends would become entitled and would receive material to which, in fact, they are not entitled if this witness is not to be admitted. And they would have that when in fact the Court determined that that was a person who should not be called and could not be called before the Court, and therefore the material that they receive is -- it would, in fact, become material to which they were never entitled. That's really the issue where we stand. That's one of the issues of where we stand. And I'm sure Mr. Emmerson will want to say that, look, that shouldn't be a reason to stop disclosure. Your Honours, we could bang on against each other all morning on these particular points, but you have before you the arguments of the parties and you will carry out as I'm sure, and I'm confident you will, and I'm sure my learned friends are of confident that you will, you will carry out the exercise in the interests of justice that we seek you to do. And there it is. I'm not going to say anymore. Mr. Emmerson looks as though he wishes to jump to his feet to make perhaps the same point again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that a fact, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I certainly don't want to make the same point again, but as soon as Mr. Rogers raises a new point that he didn't raise when he had the opportunity to respond, may I simply correct him, it is completely wrong to suggest that the Defence are not entitled to this material if in due course the Prosecution doesn't call the witness. The Defence are always entitled under the rules to disclosure in respect of each witness that the Prosecution intends to rely upon. Were this not a retrial but a trial, we would be entitled to that disclosure as of right and it would have occurred. Indeed, in respect of one witness, the Prosecution has not yet even served the witness' statement on Defence, that's 77. It is a complete misrepresentation of the position under the rules to suggest that the entitlement of the Defence to disclosure arises only at the moment that the witness is in fact called by the Prosecution at trial. Many witnesses are in the end not called, but the Defence's right to entitlement to disclosure crystallises at an earlier stage, it crystallises at the stage when it becomes necessary for the fair preparation for trial. We are at that stage this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. I believe that's the end of the submissions that the parties would like to make. Let me just indicate that I've heard what you've said Mr. Emmerson, I've heard what you've said, Mr. Rogers. As we indicated in the various e-mails that were exchanged when this issue was raised by the Defence, this is an issue that is actually before the Trial Chamber and not before the Pre-Trial Judge, and I have heard it. I've heard the submissions of the parties, I'll put this before the Chamber, and the Chamber will decide the issues as expeditiously as it possibly can, taking into account the interests of justice and balancing the issues that were raised in the submissions this morning. Thank you very much. I might sound like I'm contradicting myself in the next point, the next point I would like to raise is the point of agreed facts. Again, a point which may be bedeviled by the very fact that the appeals are still pending; however, be that as it may to the extent that it is possible for the parties to agree any further facts, I would ask the parties to and urge them to continue to do so. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate, and this rather reinforces the point I was making a moment ago, it's well understood now between the parties and I hope in communications to the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not re-opening the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not re-opening it. I'm responding to the point that you've made just a moment ago, Your Honour, that we cannot take agreed facts any further not because of the outstanding Appeals Chamber judgement, although that may effect the facts that are finally admitted, but because disclosure has not been given. Until disclosure has been given we account agree the remaining outstanding potentially agreeable facts which is another reason why with respect disclosure needs to be resolved as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have two counsel on their feet. Yes Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I avoided the last fencing match, although I concur with Mr. Emmerson. And with regard to the last match and with regard to what was just said, I cannot stress how important it is that we have full disclosure before we could begin to engage in the exercise suggested by Your Honour. It is impossible at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I note the point. Okay. I would like to deal with the status of the accused and I would like to find out from each of the accused whether you have any questions or issues you wish to bring to my attention regarding your health or the treatment you are receiving at the UNDU. We'll start with you, Mr. Haradinaj. THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ: Your Honour, everything is okay. No question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Haradinaj. Mr. Balaj. THE ACCUSED BALAJ: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything is okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Balaj. Mr. Brahimaj. THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Brahimaj. Any other items the parties wish to raise? Mr. Rogers, I see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are two matters, and one relates to Mr. Kabashi. Your Honours, I raised with my learned friends last evening that in our opinion it will be necessary to apply for a videolink to begin to receive any testimony that he may wish to give. His current position is that he does not wish to testify. We have received some explanation as to the basis for that which I have disclosed to my learned friends. I hope that they have received it. I hope there was some movement -- yes, I'm seeing nods. They have received the explanation from the individual. Your Honour, I understand from my learned friends that they will oppose any videolink application, and my question for Your Honour is should we make that application in advance of determination of these remaining issues prior to any date being set for trial, or should we wait until we know when the date set for trial is so that we can deal with it with any necessary subpoena and/or warrant application at the same time? Which leads me to my next point. I know that we are all a little uncertain as to when the actual trial date will be. The Prosecution would certainly wish for at least six weeks notice of when that trial date will be so that we can make whichever necessary applications we need to make if it's, for example, a videolink application, and also that appropriate visa and travel arrangements can be made for such witnesses as require them. I make that -- I just put that on the table now so that Your Honour is aware of the sort of time notice that we would need to ensure that that the trial could start efficiently as I understand it. It may be my learned friends require more notice than that or would wish for more notice than that, but I thought it helpful at least to indicate to Your Honours where we stand. I know it's difficult in identifying time before the Tribunal, but that is the type of notice we would need to ensure it moves smoothly on the first day. So, Your Honour, there is it is. I just wanted to put on the table the question of Mr. Kabashi so that it's before you and you are aware that there is an issue relating to him and which may effect the modalities of the proceedings before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Before I comment, I don't know whether -- yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say that as these discussion moves forward, it may well be that a solution suggests itself from the competing interests of the parties. If Mr. Rogers' request for six weeks notice were to be taken as a six week delay on top of all the other delays, then we would strongly resist it. If on the other hand that time-frame runs coterminously with the delay that we are already inevitably facing, then there is no loss of time as a result. So the solution may well be for the Trial Chamber to fix a date for trial sufficiently far in advance to be confident but by that time we will have the Appeals Chamber judgement. May I suggest hypothetically, the 1st of May. That gives the Prosecution two months, slightly longer than they are asking for, to get their tackle in order and to be ready to start the trial, and providing Your Honour and the Trial Chamber accede to the request of the Defence to order disclosure now, it also gives the Defence two months to conduct investigations. And though it will mean that my client has remained in custody for four months longer than was expected, it will keep that unjust additional delay to a minimum. All of which, with respect, points to the conclusion that the Trial Chamber should set a date, give the Prosecution notice that that is when they need to be ready, put the Defence in a position so that they can be ready for that date, and enable everyone to know that this is not a trial that is going to stall and start and sputter indefinitely throughout this year, that the Trial Chamber means to get to grips with the procedure. Now, obviously if that date has to be moved back for reasons that are unavoidable on either side, then either side can make an application to move it. But without a date, these proceedings begin to look as though they are not effectively moving forwards. But obviously if the Trial Chamber fixes a date, then we need disclosure now. So all of these different considerations, including Mr. Rogers' own latest consideration, points towards the fixing of a date on or about the 1st of May, coupled with disclosure now and notice to the Prosecution now and then what seem otherwise to be time-wasting tactics on the part of the Prosecution, I'm sure that is a not the way they were intended but that is certainly the effect that they will have, can by the Trial Chamber's own effective management of the proceedings be brought together to give these proceedings the appearance that they are entitled to have; namely, proceedings that are being conducted expeditiously, efficiently, and in that manner that secures a fair and swift trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, do you have anything to say to this point? You don't have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would agree with Mr. Emmerson, but I'd just like to add one further point in relation to fixing a trial date. It would be of great convenience to the counsel that Mr. Brahimaj would wish to act for him in the trial to have some clarity when the trial date is likely to be so that we can ensure that the counsel he has chosen are in fact available for that trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Troop. The issue that Mr. Rogers raises of videolink --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Our position is a simple one, Your Honour. The Prosecution secured a retrial in this case by complaining to the Appeals Chamber that two witnesses could not be called and were not called by the Trial Chamber. The position now is that one of those two witnesses is currently continuing to be unwilling to testify. If one can put it crudely, half the justification for this retrial has disappeared. We will see what applications the Prosecution makes in terms of subpoenas and videolinks, but all of those applications were made in the original trial and resulted in a witness not claiming that he was scared but being unwilling to testify. Therefore, we will respond to such applications as the Prosecution makes and we will do so having regard to the history, to the applications that were made at the original trial which included this witness attending, refusing to testify, being warned of contempt, being held in contempt, a videolink order, testifying -- being brought to testify again, still refusing to testify. Your Honour has a very sorry history to deal with with this witness, and we will look and see in due course what applications the Prosecution makes and we will respond to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, and may I suggest we don't deal with the application just yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We -- let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It is in a sense for the the Prosecution to determine when is the right time to make its application, and no doubt it is in close contact with the lawyers acting for Mr. Kabashi both in this Tribunal and in the United States who, one would hope, after an interval of several years now have had an adequate opportunity to give their client fully informed legal advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I raise the point, the point I wanted to ask was, and I understand that when a motion for videolink is being filed it is appropriate to have a date of hearing mentioned in it. The way I heard Mr. Rogers when he raised the point, it sounded to me like the Defence is opposed to videolink in principle, and I wanted to find out if is it not possible and practical to file a motion in principle to call Mr. Kabashi by videolink and put your arguments there, even if there is no date, and let the parties make their submission. Let's flesh out the principle of the videolink hearing, what the Defence objects to, and why the Prosecution want it. Then we can give a decision in principle. Comes the time when a date is set and I don't know whether he is going to be testifying on the first day of trial, but a date can be given to him when is he going to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I see no reason in principle providing the Prosecution is in a position to update the Defence and Trial Chamber on precisely what steps are being taken in relation to communicating with Mr. Kabashi and his lawyers and everybody is fully informed. If that's the case I see no reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine that they would make their submissions, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I don't know how they plan to conduct their -- how to prosecute this application for --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, and may I simply add this: That of course it can be done in principle, equally it can be done with a hypothetical date. So were the Trial Chamber to accede to the suggestion that I make of the 1st of May as the effective start of the trial, the 4th of May could be set as a date for Mr. Kabashi's first attempt to testify. But if experience of the past trial is anything to go by, there will have to be several attempts made before the Prosecution either is in a position to call him or to abandon him. So an early date within the trial would be sensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not anticipate that. I guess the idea is we can get a principled decision on whether or not videolink is going to be used and what problems the Prosecution encounter, if any, in securing the attendance of Mr. Kabashi. That is their problem. They will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, what I was simply seeking to emphasise, and I hope that in the way in which this issue has matured during the course of this Status Conference, there was a very practical suggestion on the table for the Trial Chamber as a whole to consider which is to fix a start date of the 1st of May, and were that the case, there's no reason why the application for Mr. Kabashi needs to be made in the abstract. It can be made with a date for calling him in mind, and let's see what the colour of the Prosecution's cloth really is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Emmerson that's still in the abstract because it's a hypothetical date. You don't know whether you are going to be sitting on the 1st of May. You are saying assuming we are able to sit on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm inviting the Trial Chamber to go further and to fix the 1st of May as the trial date. And if either party needs to apply to vacate it then they can do so with reason. I'm inviting, I think with the support of all the accused, the Trial Chamber to fix the 1st of May as the start date for the trial and all parties thereafter to work to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll put it before the Trial Chamber, we'll find out. Thank you. Mr. Rogers, when you introduced this point, you then said you moved to the next point, and I must confess to me it looked like you were saying the same point in different words. Would you like to repeat the next point that you were raising that you said was related to this one of videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It really is just about notice. I was asking when should we make the application and it's linked, of course, to the notice required in relation to the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, since I've had the opportunity to make -- just make a comment, Mr. Emmerson suggested that the Prosecution may be indulging in time-wasting tactics, those are the words that he used. Your Honour, we're not in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He did say -- he doesn't say it is intended but it may seem like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yeah, a tactic is usually intentional, and Your Honour, we are not indulging in any form of time-wasting tactics, and I hope that my learned friends will not repeat such a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what I suggested is that the way the Prosecution is conducting itself is wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: We don't need to go on about it, I've made my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have made your point, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, and six weeks notice was just six weeks notice so that we can get matters up and ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. And am I right to say that if we filed a motion in principle --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- that would do it because we can do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can file that motion tomorrow, and whenever he comes, the decision has been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I hope you won't ask us to file it tomorrow. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying tomorrow, but I'm saying as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, we can put a motion together. Your Honour, I raise one other matter with that and that is that it may be that there are some issues relating to the -- to this particular application related to videolink from which you may need to hear from the United States authorities. Having spoken with them about practicalities and management of this particular application, then Your Honour may need to hear from them as to how that can be put into effect. Obviously the Defence would have access to any filing that they made, but I make mention of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It just seems to make the point even stronger that the sooner we file the motion, the better. And I would imagine that you'll facilitate our communication with the United States officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Rogers. Are you done with your items, Mr. Rogers, before I turn to Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, just on that last point so that the Chamber is aware, we've been in this world before as well, and I believe that part of what the issue will be deals with some matters of law as they relate to what remedies exist in the United States for a witness in the position that Mr. Kabashi has taken. There's a whole other question that will have to be attended to apart from the niceties of whether or not a videolink is available to the Prosecution or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true. And I would imagine that all that would be fleshed out in the submissions of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What I wanted to find out from the Defence starting with you, Mr. Emmerson, is there any other issue that you would like to raise with --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I almost said "with the Chamber," that's why I got stuck.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think if I may say so, everything hinges on the Trial Chamber now fixing a prompt trial date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith, any issue that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not at this time, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then a date for the next Status Conference will be set in due course, and there being no further issues to raise the Court will adjourn sine die.
